name: pySBD English Golden Rules Set (GRS)
origin: Golden Rules Set by the TM-Town team for Pragmatic Segmenter (https://github.com/diasks2/pragmatic_segmenter), as adapted by pySBD.
license: MIT (pySBD, Copyright (c) 2019 Nipun Sadvilkar; Pragmatic Segmenter is also MIT). Cases reproduced unmodified.

cases.text: Hello World. My name is Jonas.
What is your name? My name is Jonas.
There it is! I found it.
My name is Jonas E. Smith.
expected: My name is Jonas E. Smith.

cases.text: Please turn to p. 55.

cases.rule: Two letter lower case abbreviations in the middle of a sentence
cases.text: Were Jane and co. at the party?
expected: Were Jane and co. at the party?

cases.rule: Two letter upper case abbreviations in the middle of a sentence
cases.text: They closed the deal with Pitt, Briggs & Co. at noon.
expected: They closed the deal with Pitt, Briggs & Co. at noon.

cases.rule: Two letter lower case abbreviations at the end of a sentence
cases.text: Let's ask Jane and co. They should know.

cases.rule: Two letter upper case abbreviations at the end of a sentence
cases.text: They closed the deal with Pitt, Briggs & Co. It closed yesterday.
expected: They closed the deal with Pitt, Briggs & Co.

cases.text: I can see Mt. Fuji from here.
expected: I can see Mt. Fuji from here.

cases.text: St. Michael's Church is on 5th st. near the light.
expected: St. Michael's Church is on 5th st. near the light.

cases.text: That is JFK Jr.'s book.

cases.rule: Multi-period abbreviations in the middle of a sentence
cases.text: I visited the U.S.A. last year.
expected: I visited the U.S.A. last year.

cases.rule: Multi-period abbreviations at the end of a sentence
cases.text: I live in the E.U. How about you?
I live in the U.S. How about you?

cases.rule: U.S. as non sentence boundary with next word capitalized
cases.text: I work for the U.S. Government in Virginia.
expected: I work for the U.S. Government in Virginia.

cases.text: I have lived in the U.S. for 20 years.
expected: I have lived in the U.S. for 20 years.

cases.rule: A.M. / P.M. as non sentence boundary and sentence boundary
cases.text: At 5 a.m. Mr. Smith went to the bank. He left the bank at 6 P.M. Mr. Smith then went to the store.
expected: At 5 a.m. Mr. Smith went to the bank.
He left the bank at 6 P.M.
Mr. Smith then went to the store.

cases.text: She has $100.00 in her bag.
She has $100.00. It is in her bag.
He teaches science (He previously worked for 5 years as an engineer.) at the local University.
expected: He teaches science (He previously worked for 5 years as an engineer.) at the local University.

cases.text: Her email is Jane.Doe@example.com. I sent her an email.
The site is: https://www.example.50.com/new-site/awesome_content.html. Please check it out.
She turned to him, 'This is great.' she said.
expected: She turned to him, 'This is great.' she said.

cases.text: She turned to him, "This is great." she said.
expected: She turned to him, "This is great." she said.

cases.rule: Double quotations at the end of a sentence
cases.text: She turned to him, "This is great." She held the book out to show him.
expected: She turned to him, "This is great."
She held the book out to show him.

cases.text: Hello!! Long time no see.
Hello?? Who is there?
Hello!? Is that you?
Hello?! Is that you?

cases.rule: List (period followed by parens and no period to end item)
cases.text: 1.) The first item 2.) The second item

cases.rule: List (period followed by parens and period to end item)
cases.text: 1.) The first item. 2.) The second item.

cases.rule: List (parens and no period to end item)
cases.text: 1) The first item 2) The second item

cases.rule: List (parens and period to end item)
cases.text: 1) The first item. 2) The second item.

cases.rule: List (period to mark list and no period to end item)
cases.text: 1. The first item 2. The second item

cases.rule: List (period to mark list and period to end item)
cases.text: 1. The first item. 2. The second item.
• 9. The first item • 10. The second item
⁃9. The first item ⁃10. The second item
a. The first item b. The second item c. The third list item
You can find it at N°. 1026.253.553. That is where the treasure is.
expected: You can find it at N°. 1026.253.553.
That is where the treasure is.

cases.rule: Named entities with an exclamation point
cases.text: She works at Yahoo! in the accounting department.
expected: She works at Yahoo! in the accounting department.

cases.rule: I as a sentence boundary and I as an abbreviation
cases.text: We make a good team, you and I. Did you see Albert I. Jones yesterday?
expected: We make a good team, you and I.
Did you see Albert I. Jones yesterday?

cases.text: Thoreau argues that by simplifying one’s life, “the laws of the universe will appear less complex. . . .”
expected: Thoreau argues that by simplifying one’s life, “the laws of the universe will appear less complex. . . .”

cases.text: "Bohr [...] used the analogy of parallel stairways [...]" (Smith 55).
expected: "Bohr [...] used the analogy of parallel stairways [...]" (Smith 55).

cases.rule: Ellipsis as sentence boundary (standard ellipsis rules)
cases.text: If words are left off at the end of a sentence, and that is all that is omitted, indicate the omission with ellipsis marks (preceded and followed by a space) and then indicate the end of the sentence with a period . . . . Next sentence.
expected: If words are left off at the end of a sentence, and that is all that is omitted, indicate the omission with ellipsis marks (preceded and followed by a space) and then indicate the end of the sentence with a period . . . .

cases.rule: Ellipsis as sentence boundary (non-standard ellipsis rules)
cases.text: I never meant that.... She left the store.
I wasn’t really ... well, what I mean...see . . . what I'm saying, the thing is . . . I didn’t mean it.
expected: I wasn’t really ... well, what I mean...see . . . what I'm saying, the thing is . . . I didn’t mean it.

cases.text: One further habit which was somewhat weakened . . . was that of combining words into self-interpreting compounds. . . . The practice was not abandoned. . . .
expected: One further habit which was somewhat weakened . . . was that of combining words into self-interpreting compounds.
